title: How a client builds a chain
summary: Name matching, key identifiers and signature checks, step by step up to a trust anchor.

steps.title: The client's algorithm
body: When your browser or `HttpClient` receives a certificate, it runs roughly this loop:
2. Find a candidate issuer: a certificate whose **Subject** equals the leaf's **Issuer** (and, if present, whose
**Subject Key Identifier** equals the leaf's **Authority Key Identifier**). Candidates come from what the server sent,
3. **Verify the signature** on the current certificate using the candidate's public key. Names can be forged; signatures cannot.
4. Check the candidate is allowed to issue: `CA:TRUE`, Key Usage `Certificate Sign`, within any `pathlen`, and in its validity period.
5. Move up to the candidate and repeat, until you reach a certificate that is in the **trust store** (a *trust anchor*).
6. Finally check every certificate's dates, the leaf's hostname and EKU, and (optionally) revocation.
If step 2 finds nothing, the chain is **partial**. If it ends at a self-signed root that isn't in the trust store, the root is **untrusted**.

prompt: Put the chain-building steps in order.
lines: Take the leaf certificate the server presented
Look for a certificate whose Subject matches the leaf's Issuer
Verify the leaf's signature with that candidate's public key
Check the candidate is a CA allowed to sign certificates
Repeat one level up until reaching a certificate in the trust store
Check dates, hostname and usage across the finished chain
steps.explain: Name matching only *finds* a candidate. The signature check is what proves the link.

steps.prompt: Why does the client verify the signature instead of just trusting that the Issuer name matches?
options: Anyone can create a certificate that *claims* any issuer name; only the real issuer's private key can make the signature verify
Names are case-sensitive and often mismatch
Signature checks are faster than string comparisons
steps.explain: An attacker can self-sign `Issuer: CN=DigiCert Global Root G2` in seconds. It's the signature, made with a private key they don't have, that fails.

steps.title: Key identifiers: telling same-named CAs apart
body: CAs renew. After a renewal there can be **two** certificates called `CN=Example Issuing CA 2`, with different keys.
The name alone can't say which one signed a leaf. Two extensions solve it:
- **Subject Key Identifier (SKI)**: an ID of *this* certificate's public key (usually a hash of it).
- **Authority Key Identifier (AKI)**: the SKI of the *issuer's* key, copied into the child when it was signed.
leaf     Issuer: CN=Example Issuing CA 2    AKI keyid: 9F:3B:...
old CA   Subject: CN=Example Issuing CA 2   SKI: 41:C2:...
new CA   Subject: CN=Example Issuing CA 2   SKI: 9F:3B:...   <- this one
The chain builder prefers the candidate whose SKI equals the child's AKI, then confirms with the signature.

steps.prompt: A leaf has `Authority Key Identifier: keyid:7A:0E:51`. Which candidate issuer should the client try first?
code: leaf:        Issuer: CN=Contoso Issuing CA     AKI: 7A:0E:51
Candidate 1: Subject: CN=Contoso Issuing CA    SKI: 22:B9:04
Candidate 2: Subject: CN=Contoso Issuing CA    SKI: 7A:0E:51
options: Any of them: only the name matters
steps.explain: Candidate 2's Subject Key Identifier equals the leaf's AKI. Candidate 3 has the right key ID but the wrong name, so it can't be the issuer (its name must match the leaf's Issuer too).

steps.prompt: Match each field to its role in chain building.
pairs: the name that must match it
the ID of the key that signed the child
the ID of the parent's own key

steps.prompt: `DojoCert` adds an SKI to every certificate and an AKI to every issued one. `SubjectKeyIdentifier` is a hex string; `KeyIdentifier` is bytes. What does this print?
code: var root = DojoCert("CN=Dojo Root", null, true);
var oldCa = DojoCert("CN=Dojo Issuing CA", root, true);
var newCa = DojoCert("CN=Dojo Issuing CA", root, true);
static X509Certificate2 DojoCert(string subject, X509Certificate2? issuer, bool isCa, string? dns = null, string? eku = null, int nbYear = 2030, int naYear = 2035)
var req = new CertificateRequest(subject, key, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256);
req.CertificateExtensions.Add(new X509KeyUsageExtension(isCa ? X509KeyUsageFlags.KeyCertSign | X509KeyUsageFlags.CrlSign : X509KeyUsageFlags.DigitalSignature, true));
if (dns != null) { var b = new SubjectAlternativeNameBuilder(); foreach (var d in dns.Split(',')) b.AddDnsName(d); req.CertificateExtensions.Add(b.Build()); }
if (eku != null) req.CertificateExtensions.Add(new X509EnhancedKeyUsageExtension(new OidCollection { new Oid(eku) }, false));
using var pub = req.Create(issuer, nb, na, serial);
steps.explain: Same name, different keys. The AKI in the leaf points at exactly one of them.

steps.title: Find the issuer
prompt: Write `X509Certificate2? FindIssuer(X509Certificate2 child, List<X509Certificate2> candidates)` that returns the
candidate that issued `child`, using what a chain builder uses first:
- the candidate's Subject Key Identifier equals the child's Authority Key Identifier.
Return `null` if no candidate matches. You may assume every test certificate has both extensions.
Get the hex strings like this:
hints: Compute the child's AKI once, then loop over the candidates.
Both conditions must hold: `c.Subject == child.Issuer && ski == aki`.
template: using System.Security.Cryptography;
using System.Security.Cryptography.X509Certificates;
{{CODE}}
var dojoRoot = DojoCert("CN=Dojo Root", null, true);
var dojoOld = DojoCert("CN=Dojo Issuing CA", dojoRoot, true);
var dojoNew = DojoCert("CN=Dojo Issuing CA", dojoRoot, true);
var dojoOther = DojoCert("CN=Other CA", dojoRoot, true);
var dojoLeaf = DojoCert("CN=shop.example", dojoNew, false);
var dojoFound = FindIssuer(dojoLeaf, new List<X509Certificate2> { dojoOther, dojoOld, dojoNew });
Dojo.Check("picks the renewed CA, not the old one with the same name", dojoFound != null && dojoFound.RawData.SequenceEqual(dojoNew.RawData), "matched the wrong candidate (or none)");
var dojoFound2 = FindIssuer(dojoNew, new List<X509Certificate2> { dojoLeaf, dojoRoot });
Dojo.Check("finds the root as issuer of the CA", dojoFound2 != null && dojoFound2.RawData.SequenceEqual(dojoRoot.RawData), "expected the root");
Dojo.Check("returns null when the issuer is missing", FindIssuer(dojoLeaf, new List<X509Certificate2> { dojoOld, dojoOther }) == null, "only the old CA (wrong key) and an unrelated CA were offered");
static X509Certificate2 DojoCert(string subject, X509Certificate2? issuer, bool isCa, string? dns = null, string? eku = null, int nbYear = 2030, int naYear = 2035)
var key = ECDsa.Create(ECCurve.NamedCurves.nistP256);
var req = new CertificateRequest(subject, key, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256);
req.CertificateExtensions.Add(new X509BasicConstraintsExtension(isCa, false, 0, true));
req.CertificateExtensions.Add(new X509KeyUsageExtension(isCa ? X509KeyUsageFlags.KeyCertSign | X509KeyUsageFlags.CrlSign : X509KeyUsageFlags.DigitalSignature, true));
req.CertificateExtensions.Add(new X509SubjectKeyIdentifierExtension(req.PublicKey, false));
if (dns != null) { var b = new SubjectAlternativeNameBuilder(); foreach (var d in dns.Split(',')) b.AddDnsName(d); req.CertificateExtensions.Add(b.Build()); }
if (eku != null) req.CertificateExtensions.Add(new X509EnhancedKeyUsageExtension(new OidCollection { new Oid(eku) }, false));
var nb = new DateTimeOffset(nbYear, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero);
var na = new DateTimeOffset(naYear, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero);
if (issuer == null) return req.CreateSelfSigned(nb, na);
req.CertificateExtensions.Add(X509AuthorityKeyIdentifierExtension.CreateFromCertificate(issuer, true, false));
var serial = RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes(8); serial[0] &= 0x7F;
using var pub = req.Create(issuer, nb, na, serial);
return pub.CopyWithPrivateKey(key);
